intro: Trigonometry studies relationships between angles and side lengths. It starts with right triangles, then extends the same ratios to any angle through the unit circle and graphs of sine, cosine and tangent. These lessons also introduce basic identities and how to solve triangles when some sides or angles are known.

sections.p: An angle is formed by two rays sharing a vertex. In standard position on the coordinate plane, the initial side lies on the positive x-axis; positive angles rotate counterclockwise.
A full turn is 360° or 2π radians. Convert: radians = degrees × (π/180); degrees = radians × (180/π). Common: 180° = π, 90° = π/2, 45° = π/4, 30° = π/6, 60° = π/3.
sections.code:

60° = π/3 rad
π rad = 180°

sections.p: Angles that share the same terminal side differ by full turns: θ and θ + 360°k (or + 2πk) for integer k. Example: 30° and 390° are coterminal.
The acute angle between the terminal side and the x-axis. It helps evaluate trig functions of angles outside the first quadrant.

lessons.title: Right-triangle trig

sections.p: In a right triangle, for an acute angle θ: opposite side faces θ; adjacent is next to θ (not the hypotenuse); hypotenuse is the longest side (opposite the right angle).
sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse; cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse; tan θ = opposite/adjacent. Memory aid: SOH-CAH-TOA.

cos θ = adj/hyp
tan θ = opp/adj

lessons.title: The unit circle

sections.p: The unit circle is x² + y² = 1. For angle θ in standard position, the terminal ray meets the circle at (cos θ, sin θ). That defines sine and cosine for all real θ, not only acute angles.
QI: sin+, cos+. QII: sin+, cos−. QIII: sin−, cos−. QIV: sin−, cos+. Tangent is sin/cos where cos ≠ 0.
Because the point lies on the circle: cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 for all θ.

lessons.summary: Extending sine and cosine to any angle via a circle of radius 1.

lessons.title: Sine and cosine graphs

sections.p: y = sin x oscillates between −1 and 1 with period 2π, starting at 0. y = cos x is the same wave shifted left by π/2 (starts at 1).
For y = A sin(Bx − C) + D (B > 0): |A| is amplitude; period is 2π/B; phase shift is C/B; vertical shift is D.
Amplitude is half the distance from max to min. Period is the horizontal length of one full cycle. Midline is the horizontal line through the middle (value D).
cos x = sin(x + π/2). Same shape; different starting point on a cycle.

lessons.title: Tangent and its graph

sections.p: tan θ = sin θ / cos θ wherever cos θ ≠ 0. On the unit circle that is where x ≠ 0, i.e. θ ≠ π/2 + πk.
Tangent has period π (not 2π). Vertical asymptotes where cosine is zero. Between −π/2 and π/2, tan goes from −∞ to ∞, passing through 0 at 0.

sections.p: tan(−θ) = −tan θ. The graph is rotationally symmetric about the origin.

lessons.title: Identities introduction

sections.p: An identity is an equation true for all allowed values of the variable. Trig identities rewrite expressions without changing values — useful for simplifying and solving equations.
cos²θ + sin²θ = 1. Divide by cos²θ: 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ. Divide by sin²θ: cot²θ + 1 = csc²θ.

sections.code:
csc θ = 1/sin θ
sec θ = 1/cos θ
cot θ = 1/tan θ = cos θ/sin θ
tan θ = sin θ/cos θ

sections.p: cos(−θ) = cos θ (even). sin(−θ) = −sin θ and tan(−θ) = −tan θ (odd).

sections.code: (1 − cos²θ)/sin θ = sin²θ / sin θ = sin θ   (sin θ ≠ 0)

lessons.title: Solving triangles

sections.p: Solving a triangle means finding all unknown sides and angles. For right triangles, SOH-CAH-TOA plus the fact that acute angles sum to 90° is enough when you know two pieces of data (with at least one side).
In any triangle: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Useful for ASA, AAS and sometimes SSA (ambiguous case).

sections.p: c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C. Generalizes Pythagoras (when C=90°, cos C=0). Useful for SAS and SSS.
In any Euclidean triangle, A + B + C = 180°. Once two angles are known, the third is determined.

lessons.title: Applications

sections.p: Trig shows up wherever angles meet lengths: surveying, navigation, ramps, and waves. The same ratios apply; only the story changes.
From a point d meters from a tree base, the angle of elevation to the top is θ. Height h = d tan θ (level ground).
Looking down from a height, the angle below horizontal equals the elevation angle in the right triangle formed with the ground (alternate interior angles with a transversal).
A vertical displacement like y = A sin(ωt) models simple oscillation: amplitude A, angular frequency ω. Period T = 2π/ω. This links the sine graph lesson to physics.

lessons.summary: Heights, bearings and simple harmonic ideas.
